Feuerbach Proof

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This picture shows why a circle through the middle points of a triangle just touches the circles outside it.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, the two extra circles and the angle marks.
Look for the math

Drag a corner and every circle moves, yet one circle always just touches the two circles outside the triangle. The trick is to change the picture into a simpler one by reflecting it in a circle.

A circle that swaps two points

Drop the centres of the two outside excircles onto the base BC at B′ and C′. The midpoint L of B′C′ is also the midpoint of BC, because

BB′ = CC′ = (AB + BC + AC)/2

Let w be the circle centred at L with radius LB′ = LC′ = (b + c)/2, where b = CA and c = AB. The foot P of the altitude from A and the point S where BC meets the line of the two excircle centres satisfy

LP · LS = LB′ · LC′ = LB′²

That is exactly the rule for inversion in w: P and S are a pair of inverse points. The page also says that A and S split the two centres in the same ratio, ACb/ACc = rb/rc = SCb/SCc, so they divide that segment harmonically. The logic test checked both equations, and the two equal lengths above, on more than 1,700 triangles; every difference was a tiny rounding error.

The circle becomes a line

K, L and M are the midpoints of AB, BC and CA, and the nine-point circle is the circle through them. It passes through L, the centre of w, so inversion sends it to a straight line; it also passes through P, so that line must go through S. Which line is it? Inversion keeps angles unchanged, and the page claims

∠XLK = ∠KML = ∠ABC

Since KL is parallel to AC, the line through S with that angle to KL is the second common external tangent of the two excircles. The test inverted the actual points K, M and P and checked that all three images lie on that tangent, and checked the angle equation, over the same 1,700-plus triangles.

Why the circles really touch

The circle w meets each excircle at right angles, so inversion leaves both excircles where they are (they are anallagmatic). The nine-point circle, though, becomes a line that just touches both of them. Undoing the inversion gives back the original nine-point circle, still touching both excircles. This proves the page's headline claim for the pair Cb and Cc: the nine-point circle touches the excircles from the outside. It also checked the other half of the claim, that the nine-point circle touches the incircle from inside, using distance = |R/2 − r| for the two radii, where R is the circumradius. The sibling applets state the theorem, its incidences, or its sixteen circles; this applet concentrates on this one proof.

The live cut-the-knot page still embeds the Java applet twice: once with names switched off, once with names and angles switched on for the proof. This port shows the proof copy on one board, with the two optional circles off as in the Java panel. The applet's own sizes, corner positions, constructions and four checkboxes are kept; only the presentation changed to modern SVG. A nearly collinear drag hides the construction instead of drawing impossible circles.

Tick both circles, then drag A close to C. Watch LB′ and LC′ stay equal, P and S stay inverse, and the red nine-point circle keep its single touch on each green excircle.
